qs.q: Villous adenomas of the colon are clinically significant because they:
o: They are associated with a high risk of transformation to colorectal carcinoma
They are caused by persistent infection with human papillomavirus 16
They spontaneously regress completely without any medical intervention
They exclusively occur within the proximal ascending colon region
qs.e: Villous adenomas have the highest malignant potential among colorectal polyps, with a significant risk of transformation. They are distinct from HPV-driven lesions.
qs.s: Dr. Irungu Sent SEM 2 — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man has a firm, ulcerated sigmoid colon mass. Biopsy demonstrates atypical glands invading through the muscularis propria. Which histological feature most strongly defines this lesion as malignant?
o: High mitotic activity
Cellular pleomorphism
Invasion through basement membrane
Hyperchromatic nuclei
qs.e: Pleomorphism, mitoses, and hyperchromasia can also occur in dysplasia, but invasion through the basement membrane is what actually defines malignancy. Other features alone are insufficient to confirm cancer.
qs.s: Pathology by Dr. Irungu — Study Notes — Oncopathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old man undergoes screening colonoscopy, which reveals a sessile lesion in the sigmoid colon. Histological examination shows dysplastic changes confined within the lamina propria without invasion through the muscularis mucosae. What are the two most important prognostic factors for malignant colorectal adenocarcinomas that eventually develop from such precursors?
o: Depth of invasion and presence of lymph node metastases
Total number of polyps and patient age at initial onset
Histological grade of differentiation and mucin production
Presence of perineural invasion and tumor location
qs.e: The depth of tumor invasion into the bowel wall and the presence of regional lymph node metastases are the two most crucial prognostic determinants for colorectal adenocarcinoma. While histological grade matters, depth and nodal status dictate staging and long-term survival.

qs.q: Genetic screening of a young adult with a family history of colorectal cancer reveals a germline mutation in the APC gene. The patient is found to have over 100 adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. Without prophylactic colectomy, what is the clinical trajectory of this condition?
o: Near-certain development of colorectal cancer by age 30
Spontaneous regression of adenomatous polyps by early adulthood
Transformation exclusively into benign inflammatory lesions
Development of widespread upper respiratory tract tumors
qs.e: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is caused by an APC gene mutation leading to numerous adenomatous polyps and a near-certain risk of colorectal cancer by age 30 if untreated. This contrasts with HNPCC which presents with fewer polyps and microsatellite instability.

qs.q: A research scientist studies a human colon cancer cell line and discovers a mutation in the TP53 gene. Which of the following normal functions of wild-type TP53 is most directly impaired by this mutation?
o: Inducing transcription of the pro-apoptotic gene BAX following DNA damage
Directly phosphorylating cyclin-dependent kinases to speed up G1/S transition
Forming an apoptosome complex with cytochrome c and APAF-1 in cytoplasm
Stabilising HIF-1 alpha under hypoxic conditions to promote angiogenesis
qs.e: Wild-type TP53 acts as the guardian of the genome by activating p21 for cell cycle arrest, GADD45 for repair, and BAX to trigger apoptosis when DNA damage is irreparable. It does not phosphorylate CDKs directly, nor does it form the cytoplasmic apoptosome.
qs.s: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Cell Cycle, Apoptosis & Angiogenesis — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which inflammatory bowel condition is characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation affecting exclusively the colon and rectum?
o: Crohn's Disease
Ulcerative Colitis
Gastroparesis
Diverticulitis
qs.e: Ulcerative Colitis features continuous mucosal inflammation limited to the colon and rectum only. Crohn's disease, by contrast, involves transmural inflammation that can affect any part of the GI tract.
qs.s: Clinical Chemical Pathology Crash Course — Part 2: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy for a change in bowel habits and is found to have an annular, 'napkin-ring' constricting mass in the sigmoid colon. How does this left-sided lesion typically present compared to right-sided tumours?
o: With occult bleeding and profound microcytic anaemia
With early bowel obstruction and blood-streaked stool
By remaining completely asymptomatic until metastasis
With extensive exophytic masses that tolerate growth
qs.e: Left-sided colorectal carcinomas form annular, 'napkin-ring' constricting lesions within a narrower lumen, leading to earlier presentation with obstruction and blood-streaked stool. Right-sided tumours have a wide lumen, allowing large exophytic growth before presenting with occult bleeding.
qs.s: Ovarian & Colorectal Cancer: Risks, Pathogenesis, Staging — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Approximately how much fluid does the normal colon absorb daily to help prevent diarrhea?
o: A. 90% of the total daily fluid load entering the GI tract
B. 90% of the remaining fluid load left after small intestinal absorption
C. Exactly 100 to 200 ml per day of the fluid load
D. Up to 8,000 ml per day of the total fluid load
qs.e: The colon absorbs 90% of the remaining fluid load, which is about 900 ml/24 hours, leaving a small volume to be excreted in feces. The small intestine absorbs the initial 90% of the total fluid load.

ai.summary: The colon is the major part of the large intestine, extending from the cecum to the rectum. It is responsible for water and electrolyte absorption and the formation and propulsion of feces.

sections.p: The colon is the major part of the large intestine, extending from the cecum to the rectum. It is responsible for water and electrolyte absorption and the formation and propulsion of feces.

b: Ascending Colon: Retroperitoneal; extends superiorly from the cecum to the right colic (hepatic) flexure.
Transverse Colon: Intraperitoneal; suspended by the transverse mesocolon between the hepatic and splenic flexures.
Descending Colon: Retroperitoneal; extends inferiorly from the left colic (splenic) flexure to the pelvic brim.
Sigmoid Colon: Intraperitoneal; S-shaped segment suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon, terminating at the third sacral vertebra (S3).

sections.p: The colon is distinguished from the small intestine by:
b: Teniae coli: Three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle.
Haustra: Sacculations produced by the shortening of teniae coli.
Omental (epiploic) appendices: Small, fat-filled pouches of peritoneum.
Midgut (up to distal 1/3 of transverse colon): Supplied by the Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA); venous drainage to the SMV; parasympathetic supply via the Vagus nerve (CN X).
Hindgut (distal 1/3 of transverse colon to rectum): Supplied by the Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA); venous drainage to the IMV; parasympathetic supply via Pelvic Splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).
Volvulus: Twisting of the mobile segments (sigmoid or transverse) around their mesentery, leading to bowel obstruction.
Diverticulosis: Herniation of mucosa through muscular defects, most common in the sigmoid colon.
Colorectal Carcinoma: Primarily occurs in the sigmoid colon and rectum; lymphatic spread follows the arterial supply.
Small bowel: Identified by circular folds (plicae circulares) crossing the full width, whereas haustral clefts in the colon are incomplete.
Duodenum: The ascending colon is retroperitoneal like the distal duodenum, but lacks the characteristic C-shape and digestive enzyme inlets.
Abdominal X-rays: Dilated small bowel can mimic the colon if valvulae conniventes are sparse, requiring peripheral vs. central positioning for differentiation.
Referred pain: Early obstruction or inflammation in the midgut-derived colon presents as periumbilical pain rather than localized lower quadrant pain.

faq.q: What are the three cardinal features that distinguish the colon from the small intestine?
faq.a: The colon is identified by the presence of teniae coli (longitudinal muscle bands), haustra (sacculations), and appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches).

faq.q: Which parts of the colon are located intraperitoneally?
faq.a: The cecum, transverse colon, and sigmoid colon are intraperitoneal and mobile, whereas the ascending and descending colon are primarily retroperitoneal.

faq.q: Where does the transition from midgut to hindgut blood supply occur?
faq.a: The transition occurs at the distal third of the transverse colon, where the superior mesenteric artery supply ends and the inferior mesenteric artery begins.
